title: From Chaos to Choreography: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns That Actually Work — Sandipan Bhaumik

summary: Sandipan Bhaumik establishes his 18-year background in distributed data systems across regulated industries and his last 2 years deploying multi-agent AI at AWS and Databricks. His central thesis is that scaling from one to five agents is a distributed systems problem, not an AI problem, and most teams fail because they lack distributed systems thinking. He shares a production war story: a credit decisioning system with five agents where cache invalidation failure caused the risk assessment agent to read a stale credit score (680 instead of 750), resulting in 20% incorrect risk ratings and taking 2 days to diagnose. He explains coordination complexity grows exponentially: five agents have at least 10 potential connections, each a failure point. He introduces two coordination patterns. Choreography is event-driven and decentralized: agents publish and subscribe to events, making them loosely coupled but extremely difficult to debug without bulletproof observability. Orchestration is centralized: a workflow orchestrator calls agents directly, manages parallelism, retries, state, and logging, serving as the single source of truth. The decision framework uses workflow complexity and autonomy requirements as axes: choreography for simple/high-autonomy, orchestration for complex/low-autonomy, hybrid choreography-with-saga for complex/high-autonomy. He advocates immutable state snapshots with versioning over shared mutable state. Each agent produces a sealed, immutable state version stored as an append-only log; the handoff function validates schemas, increments versions, and executes the next agent with immutable state. This eliminates race conditions and enables binary search through state history for debugging. Data contracts are the other half: agents declare input-output schemas, validated at handoff boundaries, catching quality issues immediately rather than downstream. He registers these contracts in Databricks Unity Catalog for versioning and governance. He then covers failure recovery patterns. Circuit breakers wrap agent calls, failing fast after repeated failures and testing recovery with a half-open state, preventing cascading failures. The saga compensation pattern requires every agent to have execute and compensate methods; on failure, the orchestrator walks backward through successful agents calling compensate to undo work, returning to initial state. He presents a production architecture: LangGraph orchestrator as the brain, agents as Unity Catalog functions or models, Delta Lake storing immutable state versions as rows, MLflow tracing every call, and circuit breakers enforced at the serving layer via AI Gateway. He closes by emphasizing that these patterns—choreography versus orchestration, immutable state, circuit breakers—are unsexy infrastructure work that won't earn applause but makes systems reliable and prevents 2 a.m. failures. He urges the audience to be systems engineers and apply these patterns in production.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Sandipan introduces himself, his 18 years in distributed data systems across regulated industries, and his 2 years deploying multi-agent AI in production at AWS and Databricks, framing the talk around patterns that work when transitioning from single to multi-agent systems.

sections.title: The Problem: From One Agent to Five
sections.summary: Explains how adding agents introduces coordination problems—data dependencies, shared state conflicts, cascading failures—transforming an AI problem into a distributed systems problem. Shares the credit decisioning war story where cache invalidation failure caused stale reads, leading to 20% incorrect risk ratings and a 2-day diagnosis effort.

sections.title: Why Complexity Explodes
sections.summary: Coordination complexity grows exponentially: one agent has zero coordination problems, five agents have at least 10 potential connections, each a failure point. The problem is building a distributed system without distributed systems thinking.

sections.title: Choreography Pattern
sections.summary: Event-driven, decentralized coordination where agents publish and subscribe to events on a message bus. Loosely coupled and scalable but extremely difficult to debug without bulletproof observability and strong delivery guarantees. Suitable for naturally event-driven workflows with high autonomy needs.

sections.title: Orchestration Pattern
sections.summary: Centralized coordinator calls agents directly, manages parallelism, state, retries, and logging. Agents remain dumb. Preferred for complex dependencies, rollback needs, and auditability. Financial services uses orchestration almost exclusively. Implementable with LangGraph on Databricks or any DAG-based workflow tool.

sections.title: Decision Framework and Hybrid Patterns
sections.summary: Two-axis framework: workflow complexity (simple to complex) and autonomy requirements (low to high). Choreography for simple/high-autonomy, orchestration for complex/low-autonomy, hybrid choreography-with-saga for complex/high-autonomy. Agent Bricks on Databricks packages these patterns.

sections.title: State Management: The Wrong Way
sections.summary: Shared mutable state causes lost updates and race conditions. Even modern databases require explicit transactions, serializable isolation, and SELECT FOR UPDATE, which many teams neglect. Introduces immutable state snapshots with versioning as the correct approach.

sections.title: Immutable State Snapshots in Practice
sections.summary: Details the immutable state approach: state stored as append-only log with insert operations only. Each agent validates schema, checks data contract, processes, and produces a new immutable version. On failure, roll back to previous version. For debugging, trace state evolution from version one through N, enabling binary search through state history. Shows Python code with frozen AgentState class and handoff function performing schema validation, version increment, and next agent execution.

sections.title: Data Contracts Between Agents
sections.summary: Agents need explicit contracts: research agent promises output with findings, confidence score, sources, timestamp; analysis agent validates input and rejects handoffs with confidence below 0.7. Contracts catch quality issues at the boundary, not downstream. Databricks Unity Catalog can register and version these input-output schemas centrally.

sections.title: Failure and Recovery: Circuit Breaker Pattern
sections.summary: Agents will inevitably fail due to timeouts, rate limits, or crashes. Circuit breaker pattern wraps agent calls: after repeated failures (e.g., 5 times), circuit opens and fails fast. After timeout (e.g., 60 seconds), half-open state tests with one request. Prevents cascading failures and enables graceful degradation. Enforced at Databricks serving layer via AI Gateway. Every open-closed transition logged in MLflow.

sections.title: Failure and Recovery: Saga Compensation Pattern
sections.summary: Every agent has execute and compensate methods. On failure, orchestrator walks backward through successfully executed agents calling compensate to undo work. Analysis agent deletes draft recommendations; research agent clears cached data. Returns to initial state with no partial transactions. Required by financial services. Simple but essential for production multi-agent systems.

sections.title: Production Architecture on Databricks
sections.summary: LangGraph orchestrator serves as the brain with workflow engine, state store, and observability. Agents implemented as Unity Catalog functions or models, exposed via Model Serving with circuit breaker policies at AI Gateway. Delta Lake stores immutable state versions as rows. MLflow traces every call with latency, inputs, outputs, token usage. Unity Catalog governs access control, lineage, and audit. Agent Bricks packages these patterns for common use cases.

sections.title: Conclusion and Final Thoughts
sections.summary: Closes by emphasizing that choreography, orchestration, immutable state, and circuit breakers are unsexy infrastructure work that won't earn applause but make systems reliable and prevent 2 a.m. failures. Systems are what create value for businesses. Urges the audience to be systems engineers and apply these patterns in production.
